Guidance: Scripted pipelines (raw Groovy) are powerful but harder to lint, review, and secure than declarative pipelines' constrained, structured syntax.
Do: Default to declarative pipeline syntax; drop into scripted blocks (script {}) only for logic declarative can't express.
Don't: Write an entire complex pipeline in raw scripted Groovy when declarative syntax would cover it.

Keywords: jenkins agent, label, node selector, build isolation
Guidance: Running all builds on the controller node (agent any resolving to master) risks resource contention and security exposure on the node that also manages Jenkins itself.
Do: Run builds on labeled, disposable agents (containers or ephemeral VMs), never on the Jenkins controller.
Don't: Execute build steps directly on the Jenkins controller node.

Guidance: Echoing credentials to console output or hardcoding them in Jenkinsfiles leaks secrets into build logs that are often broadly readable.
Do: Use withCredentials/credentials() bindings so secrets are masked in logs and injected only into the scope that needs them.
Don't: Hardcode API tokens or passwords directly in Jenkinsfile sh steps.

Keywords: shared library, jenkins pipeline reuse, vars directory
Guidance: Copy-pasting the same 200-line Jenkinsfile across dozens of repos means a fix or policy change has to be applied everywhere by hand.
Do: Extract common pipeline logic into a versioned Shared Library imported via @Library, with per-repo Jenkinsfiles staying thin.
Don't: Maintain near-duplicate Jenkinsfiles across every repository.

Keywords: parallel stage, pipeline parallelism, build speed
Guidance: Running independent stages (lint, unit tests, security scan) sequentially wastes wall-clock time when they have no dependency on each other.
Do: Use the parallel directive to run independent, non-dependent stages concurrently.
Don't: Chain unrelated stages sequentially when they could run in parallel.

Topic: Pipeline as code in the repo
Guidance: Configuring pipeline steps through the Jenkins UI ('freestyle' jobs) leaves the build definition untracked, unreviewable, and easy to accidentally change in production.
Do: Keep the pipeline definition (Jenkinsfile) in the same repo as the code it builds, reviewed via normal PR process.
Don't: Configure build steps via the Jenkins web UI outside of version control.
Example: checkout scm // Jenkinsfile lives in repo root

Keywords: jenkins plugin, plugin sprawl, security patching
Guidance: Every installed plugin is an additional attack surface and upgrade dependency; unmaintained or rarely-used plugins are a common source of Jenkins CVEs and upgrade breakage.
Do: Periodically audit installed plugins, remove unused ones, and keep the rest patched to current versions.
Don't: Install plugins liberally and never revisit or prune the list.

Keywords: artifact retention, build discarder, disk usage
Guidance: Keeping every build's artifacts and logs forever silently fills the Jenkins controller's disk until builds start failing with no obvious cause.
Do: Configure a build discarder (retain last N builds or N days) per job to bound artifact/log storage.
Don't: Leave artifact and build log retention unbounded on high-frequency jobs.

Guidance: Without a post { failure {} } block wired to a notification channel, a broken pipeline can sit red for hours before anyone notices.
Do: Add post { success/failure/always {} } blocks that notify the right channel (Slack, email) on build outcome.
Don't: Leave a pipeline with no post-build notification on failure.

Guidance: Approving arbitrary Groovy script signatures in the Script Approval queue without review can let a malicious Jenkinsfile execute unsandboxed code on the controller.
Do: Review each Script Approval request individually; prefer pipeline steps/shared library functions over raw Groovy sandbox escapes.
Don't: Bulk-approve pending script signatures without reviewing what each one does.

Keywords: input step, manual approval, deployment gate
Guidance: Deploying straight to production with no manual approval step removes the last human checkpoint before a change reaches customers.
Do: Use the input step to require explicit human approval before production-impacting stages.
Don't: Auto-deploy every merge to main straight to production with no gate.

Keywords: docker agent, kubernetes plugin, ephemeral build agent
Guidance: Long-lived static build agents accumulate leftover state (cached deps, stray files) between builds, causing 'works on this agent only' flakiness.
Do: Use ephemeral Docker or Kubernetes-plugin agents that start clean for every build and are destroyed after.
Don't: Reuse the same long-lived VM agent across hundreds of unrelated builds.

Guidance: A pipeline with no timeout can hang indefinitely on a stuck step (waiting on a dead external service), tying up an agent slot for hours.
Do: Set a timeout at the pipeline or stage level so hung builds fail fast and free the agent.
Don't: Run pipelines with no configured timeout on any stage.
